topic: Decoding Epidemics: The Mechanics of the SIR Model
target_audience: University students (Introductory STEM or Public Health)

sections.title: Introduction: Why Do We Model Outbreaks?
sections.content: A brief overview of how epidemics spread in populations. Define the core objective: Predicting the 'peak' of infections and the impact of intervention.
sections.example: A campfire analogy: One spark (infected) hits a dry forest (susceptible), quickly turning into a wildfire (epidemic) before running out of fuel (recovered/immune).

sections.title: Prerequisite: Population Dynamics & Rates
sections.content: Establish the concept of flow. Introduce the idea that individuals transition between states at specific rates (represented as arrows in a flow diagram).
sections.example: A faucet filling a bucket: The rate of flow determines how fast the level changes. Here, 'flow' = number of people changing status per day.

sections.title: The SIR Framework: Defining the States
sections.content: Visual breakdown of the three compartments: S (Susceptible), I (Infected), and R (Recovered/Removed). Use a color-coded diagram (Green -> Red -> Blue).
sections.example: A game of Tag: Children who haven't been tagged (S), those currently 'It' (I), and those sitting out on the bench because they've already played (R).

sections.title: Mathematical Mechanics: The Transition Equations
sections.content: Explain the logic of transmission (S+I interaction) and recovery (I -> R). Visualize this using a graph: 'Infection Rate' curve vs. 'Recovery Rate' curve.
sections.example: An animated bar chart showing the S-bar shrinking, the I-bar spiking, and the R-bar steadily growing over a 30-day timeline.

sections.title: Simulation & Application: 'Flattening the Curve'
sections.content: Show how changing transmission variables (e.g., social distancing) flattens the peak of the 'I' curve. Summarize the model's predictive power for public health policy.
sections.example: Simulating a scenario where a digital population of robots reduces their contact rate, showing the Red 'Infection' peak drop significantly on the graph.
